title: Input Trust and Data Boundaries
learning_outcomes: Explain what input trust and data boundaries contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: user-controlled data.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Security begins at trust boundaries. Validate data for the intended operation, encode output for its exact context, constrain file and network access, protect credentials, and apply authorization consistently. In this lesson, focus on user-controlled data; then compare it with request headers and parameters. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use input trust and data boundaries when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Security begins at trust boundaries. Validate data for the intended operation, encode output for its exact context, constrain file and network access, protect credentials, and apply authorization consistently. For input trust and data boundaries, begin with user-controlled data. Also distinguish request headers and parameters; external api responses; database values. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: User-controlled data
items.text: Know when to use user-controlled data, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Request headers and parameters
items.text: Track where this value enters the request lifecycle and where it affects the response; client-provided data must be treated as untrusted.

items.title: External API responses
items.text: Track where this value enters the request lifecycle and where it affects the response; client-provided data must be treated as untrusted.

items.title: Database values
items.text: Keep query structure separate from data values, check failures explicitly, and use constraints or transactions when integrity depends on multiple operations.

items.title: Validating data at system boundaries
items.text: Know when to use validating data at system boundaries, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

echo implode(" -> ", $steps) . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Validate data at system boundaries and encode output for the target context; validation and escaping solve different problems.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for input trust and data boundaries from top to bottom. Start by identifying user-controlled data, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating input validation as output escaping.
common_mistakes.why: A value can be valid data and still be unsafe in an HTML or JavaScript output context.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate shape and business rules at input boundaries, then apply context-appropriate output encoding.

common_mistakes.why: A request can be sent without the original form or browser UI.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat all security-relevant validation and authorization on the server.

common_mistakes.problem: Returning internal error details to the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Stack traces and configuration values may expose sensitive information.
common_mistakes.fix: Log safe diagnostics server-side and return a generic, useful response.
